planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. China Curl performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. China Curl is a rhizomatous begonia with narrow, deeply lobed, spiraling leaves whose pointed tips curl tightly inward, giving the whole plant a wiry, twisting, almost sculptural texture unlike the broad flat leaves of most rex begonias. The dark green leaf surface carries a subtle silvery sheen and is set off by red-bristled edges, adding fine detail up close in addition to the dramatic overall spiral form. As with other rhizomatous begonias grown for foliage, small flowers are secondary and often removed to keep energy in leaf production. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by rhizome division to refresh a crowded pot.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rhizomatous Begonia Variety Classification

common_name: Curly Fireflush Begonia (Spiral-Leaf Bronze-Red Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Curly Fireflush performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Curly Fireflush is a spiral-leaved sport of the classic Fireflush begonia, its pointed leaves twisting inward at the tip while flushing a deep bronze-red along the margins that intensifies in brighter light, especially on new growth, over a base of dark olive-green. The combination of the tight spiral form and the fiery red edge coloring gives it a more dramatic, textured presence than the flat-leaved Fireflush it sported from. As with other rhizomatous begonias, small flowers are secondary to the foliage display. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by rhizome or leaf cuttings.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rhizomatous Begonia Variety Classification

common_name: Tiger Paws Begonia (Miniature Bronze-Spotted Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Tiger Paws is a compact, slow-growing begonia well suited to terrariums, dish gardens, and small pots.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Tiger Paws is a miniature rhizomatous begonia with small, rounded, chartreuse-gold leaves speckled and blotched in chocolate-bronze, resembling tiny animal paw prints scattered across each leaf, and topped with fine reddish hairs along the margins. Its diminutive size and slow, tidy growth make it a favorite for terrariums, bottle gardens, and small dish plantings where larger begonias would quickly outgrow the space. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot and rot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by leaf or rhizome cuttings to start new miniature plants.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rhizomatous Begonia Variety Classification

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Cleopatra performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Cleopatra is a classic rhizomatous begonia with distinctly star-shaped, deeply lobed leaves mottled in chartreuse-yellow and chocolate-bronze in a bold, irregular pattern, one of the most recognizable and long-cultivated foliage begonias for its unusual leaf shape as much as its color. It offsets readily from a spreading rhizome, forming a dense, low mound over time, and produces small pink flowers on tall stems above the foliage that add a light seasonal accent without detracting from the main foliage display. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot and crown rot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and divide the rhizome to propagate or refresh an overgrown clump.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rhizomatous Begonia Variety Classification

common_name: Lucerna Begonia (Classic Silver-Spotted Angel Wing Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded to partially shaded location March-May, staking the tall cane stems as needed.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil, staking the tall, jointed cane stems for support as the plant matures. Lucerna is one of the oldest and most widely grown cane-type angel wing begonias, dating to the early twentieth century, with large, olive-green, silver-spotted, wing-shaped leaves and abundant hanging clusters of coral-pink flowers that bloom for much of the year under good conditions. Its tall, upright, multi-caned growth habit forms a substantial shrubby specimen over time, more of a small tree than a compact houseplant, making it a striking backdrop plant or focal point in a shaded bed or large container. Pinch young cane tips to encourage branching and a fuller habit, water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings.
sources: American Begonia Society — Cane-Type Begonia Variety Classification

common_name: Sophie Cecile Begonia (Pink-Flowered Cane Angel Wing Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded to partially shaded location March-May, staking the tall cane stems as needed.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil, staking the jointed cane stems for support as the plant matures. Sophie Cecile is a classic cane-type angel wing begonia with medium green, silver-spotted, wing-shaped leaves and large, showy clusters of bright pink flowers that hang from the upper canes for much of the warm season, blooming more heavily than many other angel wing cultivars. Its upright, multi-caned habit forms a substantial shrubby clump over a season or two, useful as a shaded accent or backdrop plant in a bed or large container. Pinch young cane tips to encourage branching and fuller growth, water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings.
sources: American Begonia Society — Cane-Type Begonia Variety Classification

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in zone 9; Maudiae cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Grow in a small pot in a fine-bark or sphagnum-based terrestrial orchid mix that holds some moisture, since Paphiopedilum lacks the water-storing pseudobulbs of many other orchids.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — an east or shaded north window suits it well, since direct sun scorches the leaves. Maudiae is a foundational hybrid lady slipper orchid whose broad, mottled gray-green and dark green leaves are attractive year-round even without bloom, giving rise to the entire mottled-leaf Paphiopedilum breeding line that shares its name as a type designation. A single, long-lasting flower with a distinctive pouched lip appears on a slender stem, typically in cool green and white or in the darker maroon-black tones of the complex-hybrid line, and each bloom can last many weeks. Unlike epiphytic orchids, it wants a mix that retains a bit more moisture and should never fully dry out between waterings, though standing water in the crown or pot will quickly cause rot. Repot every one to two years as the fine-bark mix breaks down.

common_name: Baby Joe Joe Pye Weed (Dwarf Native Butterfly Perennial)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Baby Joe is a dwarf Joe Pye weed selection, even more compact than Little Joe, suited to smaller borders and container plantings.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Baby Joe brings the same late-summer clusters of dusty mauve-purple flowers and strong butterfly and pollinator appeal as full-sized Joe Pye weed into a truly dwarf plant, shorter even than the popular Little Joe selection, fitting compact borders, foundation plantings, and containers where taller Joe Pye species would overwhelm the space. Like its taller relatives it prefers consistently moist to wet soil and tolerates periodic standing water, making it a good choice for a rain garden edge or low spot that stays damp. Cut the plant back in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
